stories.headline: Doc Rivers: Giannis 'didn't want to be the bad guy' when seeking Bucks exit
stories.summary: Former Bucks coach Doc Rivers says Giannis Antetokounmpo "didn't want to be the bad guy" when he was trying to seek a trade out of Milwaukee last season.
stories.body:
Former Milwaukee Bucks coach Doc Rivers says Giannis Antetokounmpo kept "yo-yoing" by not publicly requesting a trade before ultimately being dealt to the Miami Heat this summer.

"Giannis wanted out, but he was a Buck. And he didn't want to be the bad guy," Rivers told "The Bill Simmons Podcast" in an episode posted Thursday. "He wanted [GM] Jon [Horst] and [owner] Wes [Edens] and those guys to say, 'We're trading you,' instead of him asking for a trade. To me, that was the game that was being played."

The 2025-26 season for the Bucks was largely overshadowed by Antetokounmpo's future with the franchise he led to the 2021 NBA championship. Throughout the season, Antetokounmpo told multiple outlets, including ESPN, that he was committed to the Bucks and would "never" demand a trade.

However, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania that Antetokounmpo and his agent, Alex Saratsis, had consistently informed the Bucks since May 2025 that he wanted a trade and believed it was best for both sides to part ways. That ended with the Bucks trading Antetokounmpo and Bobby Portis to the Heat for Tyler Herro, Kel'el Ware, Jaime Jaquez Jr., Kasparas Jakucionis, three first-round picks, one pick swap and one second-round pick.

The Heat are off to a slow start in Antetokounmpo's first season, going 3-6 through Thursday's 120-100 loss to the Golden State Warriors. Antetokounmpo is leading the Heat in points (27.3 PPG) and rebounding (12.7 RPG).

Rivers discussed the challenges of coaching Antetokounmpo, telling Simmons he wished that Antetokounmpo had stepped up as more of a leader in Milwaukee.

"Giannis needed to just give himself to the team, not to anyone else," Rivers said.

He also addressed Antetokounmpo's style of play as a unique problem.

"I liked Giannis a lot. I liked him more as a dude," Rivers told Simmons. "He's interesting. He's not easy. He's not easy because he plays at this crazy downhill pace. He's really a difficult guy. ... He has this great passing ability, but he doesn't necessarily have this super IQ at the same time. It's really a strange thing, and he really has one way: downhill, force, force. Every play, he wants to force it."

"I wish he learned how to execute better," Rivers added. "He's one of those guys ... that have never needed to execute because they can do it on their own. But that doesn't help the team. And I told Giannis this, the thing he needs to still learn is the value of execution. How important it is when you're in practice and shootarounds to lock in on execution. And now he has a coach [Erik Spoelstra] who is as good as there is in execution."

Rivers coached the Bucks for three seasons, going 97-103 with two first-round playoff exits before Milwaukee missed the postseason entirely last season for the first time since 2015-16. The day after the 2025-26 regular-season finale, the Bucks announced that Rivers would not return as coach.

An NBA champion after coaching the Boston Celtics to the 2007-08 title, Rivers reiterated to Simmons that he has no plans to coach again. He joined NBC in September to serve as an NBA analyst.

stories.headline: Who should win 2026 MLS awards: Messi for MVP? Sullivan best young player?
stories.summary: With the MLS regular season coming to an end this weekend, ESPN asked its analysts to make their choices for the league's year-end awards.
stories.byline: Jeff Carlisle and Cesar Hernandez and Lizzy Becherano
stories.body:
The 2026 MLS regular season comes to a close Saturday. So much has happened in the 259 days since the campaign began -- there was a whole FIFA World Cup in the middle of the year, remember that? -- and that unpredictability has delivered some unexpected candidates for the league's year-end awards.

Back in February, who among us thought that then-16-year-old Cavan Sullivan would play at an MVP level? Who knew that Antoine Griezmann would hit the ground running upon his long-awaited arrival in North America? Who knew that former United States interim manager B.J. Callaghan would lead Nashville SC to the Supporters' Shield?

Although, there is always one constant you can count on: Lionel Messi playing at a level that no one has ever seen before in MLS.

So, on the eve of the season's final matchday, ESPN asked its writers: Who are you picking for this year's awards? Jeff Carlisle, Cesar Hernandez and Lizzy Becherano make their selections for coach of the year, young player of the year, newcomer of the year and Landon Donovan MVP.

Coach of the year

B.J. Callaghan, Nashville SC: This category is probably the toughest to pick. The midseason turnaround put in by the Philadelphia Union's interim manager Ryan Richter has been stunning. St. Louis City's Yoann Damet has accelerated the club's turnaround, with a 19-game unbeaten streak, and a U.S. Open Cup title, although they've faded of late.

Bruce Arena has gotten the San Jose Earthquakes back to the playoffs in his second season, no small feat given the club's usual level of ineptitude. The excellent season put in by FC Dallas' Eric Quill has flown under the radar. And then there's Callaghan, who now has a major trophy on his résumé with this year's Supporters' Shield triumph.

This probably comes down to a two-man race between Richter and Callaghan. My nod goes to Callaghan given Nashville is on the cusp of a record-setting points haul this season. -- Carlisle

Marko Mitrovic, New England Revolution: Expectations were modest, at best, for the Revs as they headed into 2026 under Mitrovic. Following a 2025 season that saw them once again miss out on the playoffs thanks to their 11th-place finish in the Eastern Conference, this year was anticipated to be more of a rebuild than anything else.

Instead, what followed was plenty of defensive solidity that propelled them up to their fourth place in the Supporters' Shield standings. In attacking support, Mitrovic has also gotten the best out of Carles Gil, who leads the team in goal contributions with 25. After a few years coaching within the U.S. youth international structure, Mitrovic is now thriving at the senior level. -- Hernandez

B.J. Callaghan, Nashville SC: Callaghan undoubtedly deserves this trophy for the incredible work he's done with Nashville. The team lifted the Supporters' Shield and tied Miami's MLS regular-season points record with one game left in the campaign. He's elevated the club since joining in 2024, taking a good roster to a trophy-winning club.

"B.J. is an excellent coach, very talented coach," said Hany Mukhtar. "What impresses me most is that he's always willing to improve -- constantly willing to improve the team, constantly willing to adjust and make players better and better and better. And that is, I think, the culture at this club." -- Becherano

Young player of the year

Cavan Sullivan, Philadelphia Union: I would be shocked if my colleagues selected anybody else. Once only on the radar of American soccer nerds, Sullivan has rapidly transitioned from teenage prospect to a genuine elite MLS player in 2026.

What's especially exciting about the 17-year-old is that he's not only shining on the stats sheet with his goals and playmaking, but also showing off a compelling level of tenacity and fight for a player who is still technically a kid. He's a joy to watch, and it's only a matter of time before the rest of the world learns about the creative yet daring attack-minded player and future U.S. men's national team star. -- Hernandez

Julian Hall, Red Bull New York: This is a tough award to give with so much rising talent between Sullivan, Hall and Justin Ellis, but I have the Red Bull New York striker just narrowly edging out the others. He's developed steadily over the years, really breaking out this season under head coach Michael Bradley.

Hall has 13 goals and five assists in 31 games, becoming an integral part of the Red Bull roster. Hall also became the youngest player in MLS history to record a hat trick, doing so at 18 years and 50 days. He has so much potential to tap into yet, but he's already showing signs of stardom. -- Becherano

Cavan Sullivan, Philadelphia Union: The amount of attention attached to Sullivan's arrival in MLS as a 14-year-old would have sunk just about any player in the league at the same age. Two years on, he's grown to the point that he's begun exceeding the hype.

His six goals and ten assists in league play since the World Cup break have played a huge part in the Union's second-half revival, in which they rose from rock bottom of the league-wide standings to clinching a playoff spot. The only question heading into Decision Day is which team Philadelphia will play in the postseason. Even better, Sullivan has done it with a style that has generated a tidal wave of excitement over just how much he'll grow in the coming years. -- Carlisle

Newcomer of the year

Antoine Griezmann, Orlando City SC: Many questioned what version of Griezmann would arrive in Orlando after years of wanting to play in the U.S., but he quickly proved that he came to MLS to compete. Although he signed in March, he didn't join the team until July following the end of the LaLiga season. It took him little time to adjust, scoring just 48 minutes into his debut.

Since then, Griezmann has gone on to record 14 goals and eight assists in just 17 games. His contributions propelled Orlando from 12th place, sitting outside the playoffs upon his arrival, to clinching a place in the 2026 postseason. -- Becherano

Antoine Griezmann, Orlando City SC: This award looks to be a two-horse race. Do you go with the season-long excellence of the Houston Dynamo's Guilherme, and his 16 goals and 10 assists? Or do you opt for the second-half supernova that was Griezmann, with his 14 goals and eight assists?

Both players have vastly outperformed their xG+xA, with Guilherme by almost 13 goal contributions while Griezmann has nine more than expected, but it's hard to look past the fact that the France World Cup winner's numbers have come in about 1,000 fewer minutes. Orlando has also resurrected its playoff chances with Griezmann in the lineup, clinching a spot on Sunday. Those last two factors mean that Griezmann just edges out Guilherme for the award. -- Carlisle

Guilherme, Houston Dynamo: Some players need weeks, if not months, to adjust to MLS. Guilherme needed 66 minutes. Scoring in the second half of his debut match for Houston in February, the Brazilian then doubled the mark with a game winner that cemented a brace in his first-ever MLS game -- which foreshadowed what would eventually follow.

Since then, the 31-year-old has continued to be highly efficient with 16 goals and 10 assists across his 30 appearances. Although things have slowed down for a Houston side that have just one win in their past nine, they could still become dark horses in the playoffs if they have a healthy and fit Guilherme in the XI. -- Hernandez

Landon Donovan MVP

Lionel Messi, Inter Miami: Is there really any other choice? Numbers-wise, the Argentina World Cup winner has practically lapped the field with 26 goals and 16 assists, and Miami has done well enough as a team to make Messi's contributions vital.

To be clear, other players had outstanding seasons. There remains a chance that the best player on the best team, that being Nashville SC's Hany Mukhtar, will get some votes, but his 17 goals and eight assists don't stack up to Messi. Neither do the 14 goals and 17 assists that Evander put up for an inconsistent FC Cincinnati side. Had Griezmann been with the club for a whole season, he might have threatened Messi for MVP supremacy. But as it stands, Messi is the clear choice. -- Carlisle

Lionel Messi, Inter Miami: Surprise, surprise. Sure, there are plenty who will justifiably wonder if this is simply just a popularity vote when he once again wins this award, but the numbers don't lie.

Messi leads the league in goals, goal contributions and xA. Diving into American Soccer Analysis' Goals Added metric, which "measures a player's total on-ball contribution in attack and defense," the Argentine superstar is head and shoulders above every other player in MLS with a tally of 14.06. For reference, at second place is San Jose Earthquakes forward Preston Judd, with a tally of 4.37. No matter the fact that he'll turn 40 next year, Messi continues to be the most dominant figure in MLS. -- Hernandez

Lionel Messi, Inter Miami: For a third consecutive season, Messi deserves the MVP award. He's recorded 26 goals and 16 assists in 30 games, carrying Inter Miami to second in the Eastern Conference, the Campeones Cup win over Cruz Azul and yet another Concacaf Champions Cup qualification.

Beyond the goals and assists, Messi's vision and IQ transform Inter Miami. The Herons struggled with consistency this season, playing under three coaches in the span of one campaign, but despite the constant chopping and changing, Messi remained the only positive constant. MLS may just have to change the name of the award given that Landon Donovan only won it twice. -- Becherano

stories.headline: Does Man United's coach matter? Could Jurgen Klopp reach Premier League glory at Old Trafford?
stories.summary: If Manchester United hired an all-time great like Jurgen Klopp, would they have won the Premier League? Let's find out!
stories.body:
Right around this time every year, you can start to feel it. The air gets a little crisper. The shadows get a little colder. The days get shorter. The tree colors start to pop. You start wearing sweaters. Pumpkins appear in places where they do and do not belong.

Everyone and everything starts to shift, just slightly, in preparation for what's about to happen. The cycles of nature can be fickle and unpredictable, so the date is never exactly the same, and some years come and go without anything at all. But most years, it does.

Our tiny little rituals prime us to anticipate the inevitable, oncoming shift: that moment when Manchester United fire their manager and convince themselves that the new guy is finally going to be the one who fixes everything.

Ruben Amorim lost his job last January. Erik ten Hag was fired two years ago, right before Halloween. Ole Gunnar Solskjaer got the boot just a couple of days before Thanksgiving. And Jose Mourinho was relieved of his duties a little over a week before Christmas.

Now that we've once again entered the season of sacking, Michael Carrick seems like he will inevitably become the latest victim.

Man United are clear of the relegation zone on goal differential alone. If history is any indication, their comeback against AS Roma in the Champions League will end up being meaningless. Before Tuesday's win, Carrick appeared to be on the verge of tears at the end of every match.

This is the 14th season since Manchester United last won the Premier League. And whoever replaces Carrick will be the ninth coach to try to do something that no other United manager since has done: just, simply, meet the expectations at one of the richest sports teams on the planet for more than a single season in a row.

But given how many different coaches have now failed since Sir Alex Ferguson left the club, it makes you wonder: Could anyone have been successful at Manchester United?

What is a great manager worth?

Arsenal won the Premier League last season with 85 points.

If we lived in a world where there were no subs and everyone on the field contributed exactly evenly to their team's success, then all 11 Arsenal players would have contributed about 8 points (7.7, to be slightly more exact) of value last season.

Except, the alternative to each player isn't just zero points. If you removed Bukayo Saka from the lineup, you wouldn't have to play a man down. No, you'd get to put another player out there who would also contribute to winning to some degree.

So, let's look at the relegation-level cutoff. West Ham were relegated with 39 points. Using the same framework, we'd say that all of their players were worth a little over 3.5 points across the season. We could then say that the average Arsenal player provided 5 more points of value than a relegation-level player.

This, of course, isn't exactly how it works: Some players are better than others, some positions are more valuable than others, and almost nobody plays 100% of the minutes. Goalkeeper David Raya played 97.3% of the league minutes last season, and Declan Rice led all outfield Gunners with 90.5% of minutes played.

But it all still gives us a nice benchmark. The best players on the best teams in the world are probably worth around 7 points more than your average relegation-level player. The truly generational superstars? You could probably bump that number up to 10 points if you wanted to.

But what about the manager? Rather than litigating the whole "managers don't matter" conversation for the 1,000th time on this website, we're just going to go with the logic put forth by Liverpool's former director of research, Ian Graham, in his book, "How to Win the Premier League": "[About] the same value as a good player brings. This is in line with manager salaries -- the best managers are paid a similar wage to the best players."

Who, then, was the best manager that Manchester United could've hired at any point over the past 14 seasons?

Most soccer-watchers would agree that there are two potential answers: Pep Guardiola or Jurgen Klopp. And most analyses would agree.

A 2025 study from the Sloan Sports Analytics conference looked at team performances from 2017 through 2024 across Europe's Big Five top leagues. The study awarded or penalized the manager for how much a team's performance level exceeded or undershot expectations based on the talent of the roster. Klopp and Guardiola topped the list -- with a significant gap between themselves and the next tier of coaches.

Given the 114 guilty charges against Manchester City under Guardiola, though, I think we have to go with Klopp. While Guardiola's influence on how the sport is played is undeniable, we now have to look on his Man City tenure skeptically. We know how much they outperformed what we were told they spent, but it would be foolish to blindly accept those numbers and attribute the gap purely to the Guardiola effect.

With Klopp, though, we know that he turned two clubs that were not even the richest clubs in their own leagues into two of the best teams in the world. And we know that he maintained those levels -- at both clubs -- for many seasons in a row. On top of that, both Borussia Dortmund and now Liverpool seem to have gotten worse after he left each job.

The job of the manager, simply, is to make his team better than the talent his club can afford to acquire and then to keep that improvement going even as the roster turns over. At the highest level of the sport, Klopp was better at that than any of his peers.

Could the best manager in the world save Manchester United?

What, then, might've happened if Manchester United somehow managed to hire Jurgen Klopp back in 2013 instead of David Moyes?

There are, of course, all kinds of ripple effects we could tease out -- what it would've done to German soccer, where Liverpool would've ended up, how Mohamed Salah's career would've played out, and on and on.

But I just want to focus on what it would've meant for Manchester United. We know that Liverpool benefitted from hiring Jurgen Klopp. But we also know that Jurgen Klopp benefitted from working for a club that did things like convincing him to sign Mohamed Salah instead of Julian Brandt.

Liverpool's cutting-edge front office didn't turn the club into the best team in the world, and neither did Klopp. No, it was the combo of the two that did it.

We could say similarly about Borussia Dortmund. At the time, Dortmund were one of the leaders in both youth development and identifying young stars. This meant that Klopp got the ideal kinds of talent, energetic youngsters to play his high-pressing style: Robert Lewandowski, Mats Hummels, Marco Reus, and Ilkay Gündogan -- just to name a few.

What we know about Manchester United, broadly, is that the club is an abject disaster. In terms of doing things that increase their chances of winning games, they are pretty much as bad as it gets. Since 2013, United have finished at or higher in the table than their relative Premier League revenue ranking once -- and that was last season.

While we could employ some magical thinking and convince ourselves that the only problem here is that the club can't hire the right coach, that's obviously not true. If it were, it would mean that the club that keeps firing its coaches just so happens to be doing all of the other things right.

No, the failure to find a successful long-term coach is a symptom of all of the other issues that plague the club. They've so badly underperformed their resources for over a decade; we can confidently say there is something deeply wrong with the way Manchester United tries to build its soccer teams.

So, if Klopp were the Man United coach, he wouldn't have fixed all of those problems. No, he would've had to work within that dysfunctional environment. He would've, in other words, ended up with Brandt instead of Salah -- many times over.

But let's sketch out the absolute best-case scenario for this hypothetical. Let's say that United have continued to hire "relegation-quality" managers. And let's say that Klopp's value is equivalent not just to the best player on a title team but to a true, once-in-a-generation superstar.

Neither of those things is true -- United aren't constantly hiring genuinely bad coaches, and Klopp himself would tell you that he's not worth the same as Lionel Messi -- but stretching the effect out to the extreme helps make the point.

Plus, by applying a Messi-like effect every year, we're canceling out some of the other problems with this exercise: not addressing the Manchester City situation, not subtracting points from other teams, not accounting for the increased spending power from an increased performance level, and so on.

If Klopp could've added 10 points to every Manchester United season, here's how things would've changed:

On average, United would've ended up with 76 points per season instead of 66, and their average finishing position would've been 3.8 instead of 5.3.

So, of course: things would be better if Manchester United had employed the best manager of the modern era for the last decade-plus. In this scenario, they would've finished in the top four 10 times, rather than six. Perhaps there would've been a deep Champions League run at a club that reached three finals in four seasons from 2008 to 2011 and hasn't been beyond the quarterfinals since.

But even if we granted Manchester United 13 straight seasons of consistent, transformative, incomparable, once-in-a-generation managerial performance, the team would still find itself right where it sits today: with no Premier League titles since Sir Alex Ferguson left the club.

stories.headline: Fantasy hockey trade suggestions: Guide to the luckiest and unluckiest shooters
stories.summary: Are these hot (or cold) starts sustainable? We look at the extreme shooting percentages and trades to make.
stories.body:
Just like get-rich-quick schemes or movie star lookalikes online who insist they're really, really into you, some early-season fantasy performances are too good to be true. Or rather, too good to remain true. If that middle-pack winger is suddenly lighting it up in uncharacteristic fashion, there's reason why. Or they're off to an exceptionally lucky start. Fortunately, we have access to metrics that help expose who's finding the net more often than they realistically should. Players who you might want to move via trade before their fantasy-relevant numbers cool off.

With the help of Evolving Hockey in providing Individual Shooting Percentages (Sh%) Individual Expected Goals (ixG), we can suss out who might be overachieving in finding the back of the net this fall with a little too much help from Lady Luck. Plus a trio of current underachievers to target before they predictably erupt.

More: Rankings | Most added/dropped | Mock Draft Lobby

Draft guide | Who to keep or drop | One pick for every team | Sign up

Artturi Lehkonen, F, Colorado Avalanche(35.29 Sh%, 12 goals, 6.42 ixG): Unquestionably, the Avalanche winger is serving as a fantasy delight to launch 2026-27. Equally incontestably, there's zero chance he continues to capitalize on one-third of his shots on net. Lehkonen scored six goals in his first 16 games this past season, which falls much more comfortably within the productive scope of his 12-year career. Oh, he'll probably net a career-high 35-plus this round -- it's a contract year! -- based on the foundation of this fortuitous start. But that only amounts to another five goals or so per month. Trade Lehkonen now, while other managers remain wooed by his team-leading, double-digit tally.

Matvei Michkov, F, Philadelphia Flyers (37.04 Sh%, 10 goals, 5.13 ixG): The good news is, the 21-year-old is clearly in far superior shape to start this campaign after a disappointing showing in 2025-26. Even better for the Flyers, Travis Konecny is healthy again, along with Owen Tippett. Which is handy, considering Michkov isn't going to score another 10 goals in this coming stretch of four weeks. Wait for the skilled forward to maybe pop another goal or two, and then place him on the fantasy trade block. As far as regular skaters are concerned, only Seattle's Frederick Gaudreau has a more inflated shooting percentage at present.

Alex Tuch, F, Washington Capitals (25.64 Sh%, 10 goals, 7.46 ixG): Talk about making an excellent first impression. We're barely accustomed to seeing Tuch out of his Sabres kit (Vegas feels like eons ago now), and the new member of the Capitals is already justifying his fresh and hearty paycheck. However, the clever number crunchers tell us he should have only seven goals, not 10. Plus, other members of this very deep Washington squad are starting to heat up, and there are only so many goals to go around. Tuch could soon see his lesser share, especially if he's moved to another line at some point. Plus, he isn't skating on the top power play.

Vasily Podkolzin, F, Edmonton Oilers (27.27 Sh%, 9 goals, 5.37 ixG): It was fun while it lasted. Skating on a top line with Connor McDavid and Leon Draisaitl, and for a spell on the primary power play, Podkolzin contributed well beyond his NHL reputation. However, two goals (three assists) in 10 recent games suggests the well is drying up. Plus, that unmaintainable shooting percentage, which is the whole point of this discussion. Drop him and pick up Kasperi Kapanen -- the current placeholder for Zach Hyman on Edmonton's No. 1 power play -- or, better yet, Ryan Nugent-Hopkins, if available.

Logan Cooley, F, Utah Mammoth (30.77 Sh%, 8 goals, 5.39 ixG): In an ideal world, coach Andre Tourigny successfully encourages his rising star to shoot more on net altogether. Already in his relatively short career, the 22-year-old is displaying an undeniable knack for accuracy. If Cooley continues to pepper the net more often, as has been the case in four recent games, he'll score upwards of 45 this year. If not, and the forward hovers around the 150-shot mark once again, that ceiling drops. Food for fantasy thought when weighing his worth this season in redraft leagues.

Ready to heat up

Juraj Slafkovsky, F, Montreal Canadiens (5.75 Sh%, 2 goals, 4.50 ixG): No one wears their feelings on their face louder than the Montreal winger. Let's just say his expressions have fallen on the darker side of late. No doubt having only two goals to show for 15 games, after scoring 30 this past season, must feel very frustrating. But not to fret. Along with an inevitable turn in fortune, having Nick Suzuki back as his regular center will only expedite getting Slafkovsky back to his scoring self. Consider making his present manager an offer.

Patrick Kane, F, Chicago Blackhawks (4.00 Sh%, 1 goal, 3.3 ixG): Once back from injury, the Blackhawks veteran is going to pot more than one goal on his next 25 shots while competing alongside Connor Bedard. Promise. If you need scoring help, keep an eye on Kane's precise return date and give him a whirl in deeper leagues. The winger is currently available in about a third of ESPN Fantasy leagues.

Mark Scheifele, F, Winnipeg Jets (5.56 Sh%, 2 goals, 6.33 ixG): Scheifele scored 36 goals (67 assists) last year and 39 the previous season. Since this is a player who has averaged a 17.3 Sh% over his long career, don't be surprised if they start counting up quickly. If anything, this week's historical comeback win over the Canadiens should buoy the club as a whole. Volley his manager a proposal, sooner than later. Offer up Alex Tuch.

stories.headline: What Yankees, Mets can do this winter to meet their 2027 goals
stories.summary: The 2026 MLB season didn't go as either New York team planned. Here's how they can flip the script next year.
stories.body:
With a lockout looming on Dec. 1, the consensus across Major League Baseball is that November will be a frenetic month, similar to the lead-up to the 2021 lockout. Free agents will come off the board. Trades will be made. There will be a flurry of player movement before the league shuts down.

The action, according to sources, is expected to start as soon as next week, when the industry convenes at the general managers meetings in Las Vegas. And you can expect the two New York clubs will be involved.

The Yankees and Mets experienced very different versions of disappointment in 2026. The Yankees reached the postseason for the eighth time in nine years under manager Aaron Boone, only to get bounced by an American League East rival in the division series for the second straight year.

The Mets, meanwhile, did not make the playoffs for the second consecutive season, finishing last in the National League East despite having one of baseball's two most expensive payrolls.

Both teams will dabble in the free agent and trade markets to bolster their rosters this offseason. Here are three needs we believe each team will address to get over the hump by the time Opening Day comes around -- whenever that is.

New York Yankees
1. Rebuild the bullpen (starting with closer David Bednar?)

Pitching was not the problem for the Yankees in 2026. They led the majors in staff ERA by a good margin. But while they have a surplus of starters, they'll need to fill out their bullpen again this offseason. As it stands, left-hander Brent Headrick is the only reliever under team control for next season who had at least 17 appearances in 2026.

That could change soon. New York extended the qualifying offer to Bednar, who has until Nov. 17 to accept the one-year, $23.15 million deal. If he declines it, the Yankees could still re-sign him with a multiyear deal. The Yankees could convert their extra starters into relievers if they don't trade from the surplus. Ryan Weathers, Clarke Schmidt and Luis Gil are all candidates for the switch. Regardless, the Yankees, who have shown an elite ability to build strong bullpens without necessarily spending top dollar, will certainly add options this offseason.

2. Add a right-handed-hitting catcher

The Yankees stuck with Austin Wells despite his terrible start to the season at the plate, and their confidence in him eventually paid dividends: Wells posted a .784 OPS over the final two months. Still, the Yankees could use a viable right-handed-hitting catcher to pair with the left-handed-hitting Wells.

Ryan Jeffers -- if he doesn't accept the qualifying offer from the Minnesota Twins -- would be the best option in free agency, but would he warrant the money the Yankees would need to spend if he's only going to be on the short side of a platoon? Jeffers could DH, but the Yankees, starting with Giancarlo Stanton, already have a logjam there. Carson Kelly and Tyler Stephenson could be better options in that role at a cheaper price.

Potential options on the trade market include All-Stars Hunter Goodman and Shea Langeliers. The Colorado Rockies' asking price for Goodman at the trade deadline was high. The two-time All-Star could perhaps be had this winter with three controllable seasons remaining. Langeliers was also considered a trade candidate at the deadline until he tore the meniscus in his right knee in late July. But either option would require the Yankees to decide Wells is a backup, and that doesn't seem likely.

3. Solve second and third base

Ryan McMahon was one of the worst regulars in the majors last season, posting a 78 wRC+ in 124 games, while his usual elite defense at third base inexplicably regressed in his age-31 season. The Yankees could decide to replace him entirely or acquire a right-handed-hitting third baseman to split time with him. Amed Rosario filled that role for most of the 2026 season, but the Yankees did not trust his defense, which led to Jose Caballero getting playing time there down the stretch and into the postseason against left-handed pitchers.

Japanese star Teruaki Sato is the best third baseman on the free agent market, but he's not a great fit, considering scouts question his viability at third base, and he's a left-handed hitter with a huge strikeout rate. Otherwise, it's a barren free agent market for third basemen. On the trade front, Isaac Paredes and Royce Lewis could make sense.

At second base, the Yankees, with Jazz Chisholm Jr. a virtual lock to sign elsewhere, could opt to give the keys to Anthony Volpe or Caballero. Brandon Lowe and Luis Arraez, two left-handed hitters, are the top free agent second basemen besides Chisholm. Former Yankee Gleyber Torres is the best right-handed-hitting option available.

The trade market offers intriguing potential possibilities, including Ketel Marte, CJ Abrams and Xavier Edwards. All three would not be inexpensive to acquire but the Yankees have the player capital for such a move should they go that route.

New York Mets
1. Add starting pitching (Tarik Skubal, anyone?)

The Mets have an acute need for starting pitching. They could use a frontline starter to pair with Nolan McLean and a second-tier hurler to add to a rotation that currently isn't very deep. Besides McLean, the Mets have Christian Scott, Sean Manaea, Zac Thornton and Kodai Senga among their internal options under team control next season. That is not a championship-caliber group.

Their wish list starts with Skubal, the best player on the free agent market by a mile. The two-time Cy Young Award winner's contract is expected to break the record for annual average and total value. The number of teams that have historically engaged in that market is limited. Of those teams, the Mets have the most glaring need for an ace.

While president of baseball operations David Stearns has historically been against giving long-term deals to free agent starting pitchers in their late 20s or older, Skubal -- who turns 30 later this month -- could be the exception, with a push from owner Steve Cohen.

Other options in free agency include Michael King, Trevor Rogers, Tyler Mahle and Nick Pivetta. The Mets could re-sign Clay Holmes, who they traded at the deadline (don't expect a reunion with Freddy Peralta, the other free agent starter they dealt at the deadline). They could sign Kaima Taira or Hiromi Itoh, the top two starters coming over from Japan. Then there's the trade market, where Reid Detmers, Drew Rasmussen, George Kirby, Emerson Hancock and MacKenzie Gore could be among the players available.

2. Boost the bullpen

The Mets, after moving four relievers at the trade deadline, have several questions in their bullpen beyond closer Devin Williams. Left-hander Nate Lavender and right-hander Daniel Duarte shined when given the opportunity late in the season. Right-hander Austin Warren had strong stretches. Tobias Myers, acquired with Peralta from the Milwaukee Brewers last winter, has the potential. Reed Garrett, a mainstay in 2024 and 2025, is slated to return from Tommy John surgery after missing the entire 2026 season.

But the Mets need to strengthen the bridge to Williams in the coming months. Building strong bullpens takes creativity. Shutdown relievers can come off the scrap heap. They could be converted starters. There is no one formula. It's on Stearns to figure it out with the ample resources available to him.

3. Find a(nother) first baseman

Moving on from Pete Alonso last offseason proved disastrous for the Mets. Instead of re-signing the fan favorite, they opted to give free agent Jorge Polanco, who had never played first base in the majors, a two-year, $40 million contract. He posted a .431 OPS and minus-1.4 fWAR in just 37 games -- and just two of them at first base -- while dealing with an ankle injury that needed season-ending surgery in August. Meanwhile, Mark Vientos, another option the Mets thought could help, recorded a .652 OPS and minus-1.1 fWAR in 87 games.

The good news for the Mets is that Polanco's absence and Vientos's struggles afforded Jared Young extensive playing time for the first time in his career. Young took advantage. The left-handed hitter slashed .266/.330/.429 with nine home runs and a 1.0 fWAR in 103 games. Young was significantly better against right-handed pitchers (.793 OPS) than against left-handed pitchers (.606 OPS), which means the Mets could use a righty option. Maybe that's eventually Polanco, a switch-hitter, but there's a chance he's not ready for the start of the season. Adding a right-handed-hitting first baseman to platoon with Young would mitigate the risk.

stories.headline: São Paulo Grand Prix 2026: Race in Brazil start time, how to watch, full schedule, predictions
stories.summary: Formula 1 heads to Brazil for the São Paulo Grand Prix, a week after Kimi Antonelli was crowned world champion.
stories.body:
Formula 1 heads to Brazil for the São Paulo Grand Prix, a week after Kimi Antonelli was crowned world champion.

The Mercedes driver finished the Mexico City Grand Prix in third and made history by becoming Formula 1's youngest-ever world champion.

Red Bull's Max Verstappen won the race, with Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton behind in second.

So you don't miss a thing, here's everything you need to know for the 20th round.

- The families that built Kimi Antonelli, F1 world champion

- How Kimi Antonelli overcame George Russell, Ferrari to become F1's youngest champion

- Kimi Antonelli's historic F1 title: Every record broken and milestone reached

São Paulo Grand Prix schedule
All times in GMT

Friday, November 6

Practice One: 3.30 p.m. - 4.30 p.m.

Practice Two: 7 p.m. - 8 p.m.

Saturday, November 7

Final Practice: 2.30 p.m. - 3.30 p.m.

Qualifying: 6 p.m. - 7 p.m.

Sunday, November 8

São Paulo Grand Prix: 5 p.m.

How to watch

Every practice and qualifying session as well as the race itself will be available to watch on Sky Sports F1. The sessions are also on Sky Sports Main Event.

For non-subscribers, highlights of the São Paulo Grand Prix will be on free-to-air television on Channel 4.

In the U.S., subscribers can watch every session on Apple TV, via a new F1 channel on the platform.

Autódromo José Carlos Pace
Situated in a neighbourhood between two artificial lakes, Interlagos (which translates to "between lakes"), first opened as a race track in 1940. Formula 1 first raced at the circuit in 1972 as a non-championship race before becoming part of the calendar from 1973.

It dropped off the calendar in 1980 after its bumpy surface was considered dangerous, but F1 returned to a shortened and updated version of the circuit in 1990, which coincided with the rise of Ayrton Senna to global stardom. Senna's S at Turn 1 is one of the best overtaking spots on the track.

The circuit is one of the drivers and fans favourites. It's short, undulating nature, mixed with changing weather, often produces a blockbuster race.

São Paulo Grand Prix

Circuit: Autódromo José Carlos Pace; São Paulo, Brazil

Previous winners in São Paulo

2014: Nico Rosberg (Mercedes)

2015: Nico Rosberg (Mercedes)

2016: Lewis Hamilton (Mercedes)

2017: Sebastian Vettel (Ferrari)

2018: Lewis Hamilton (Mercedes)

2019: Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2021: Lewis Hamilton (Mercedes)

2022: George Russell (Mercedes)

2023: Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2024: Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2025: Lando Norris (McLaren)

Other key stats

First F1 race: 1973

Laps: 71 laps of 4.3km

Lap record: 1:10.540, Valtteri Bottas (2018)

Most wins: Alain Prost with six at Interlagos & Jacarepagua (1982-1984-1985, 1987-1988, 1990) and Michael Schumacher has four at this circuit (1994-1995, 2000-2002). Other winners from the current grid are Hamilton (2016, 2018, 2021), Verstappen (2019, 2023, 2024), George Russell (2022) and Lando Norris (2025).

Most poles: Ayrton Senna with six (1986, 1988-1991, 1994). Previous pole sitters on the current grid are Fernando Alonso (2005), Hamilton (2012, 2016, 2018), Russell (2022), Verstappen (2019, 2023) and Norris (2024 and 2025).

Weather forecast

The weather for the São Paulo Grand Prix is due to be cloudy during Friday's practice, with thundery showers forecast on Saturday with highs of 27°C. Sunday looks like it will be light showers, with temperatures dropping to 19°C.

What happened last time out?

Norris carried his winning momentum into Brazil and put his McLaren on pole position. The Brit then went on to take a dominant victory in Sunday's race.

He extended the lead in the drivers' championship to 24 points from teammate Piastri with three races of the season remaining.

Verstappen had a remarkable drive after struggling with the car in qualifying. For the race, the Red Bull driver started from the pit lane so the team could fit a new engine and change the car set-up, and ended up recovering to finish third.

Mercedes' Antonelli finished second, with his teammate Russell in fourth.

Who will win this year?

Antonelli clinched his maiden world title last time out, so the pressure will be off his shoulders now after getting the job done in Mexico City. He could also break a few more records including most wins in a maiden championship season.

Verstappen leapfrogged to second in the title standings and won the race last week to take his third victory this season, so could be a threat to Mercedes.

Hamilton sealed his first pole position last time out for Ferrari and looked more comfortable in the car. The seven-time world champion, who is an honorary citizen of Brazil, has always been one to watch at this track.

Despite the drivers' championship being wrapped up, the constructors' is all to play for. Mercedes are in mathematical contention to win it in Brazil and will be looking to maximise points from both Antonelli and Russell.

The team need to outscore Ferrari by three points or more.

stories.headline: The Philippine legend who keeps Jonny Parsons going
stories.summary: Philippine hero Lapu-Lapu defeated Ferdinand Magellan at the Battle of Mactan in 1521, and the story carries a personal meaning for Jonny Parsons that he takes with him every time he steps into the Octagon.
stories.body:
More than 500 years after Lapu-Lapu defeated Ferdinand Magellan at the Battle of Mactan, his legacy continues to inspire generations of Filipinos.

For UFC fighter Jonny Parsons, that story carries a personal meaning that he takes with him every time he steps into the Octagon.

Parsons, a Filipino-American whose mother is from Cebu, learned about the legendary warrior only in 2020, well into his mixed martial arts career. But once he discovered Lapu-Lapu's story, he found a connection to the resilience and spirit that have become part of his identity as a fighter.

"I have the warrior spirit," Parsons told ESPN. "My mom is from Cebu, so I have that Lapu-Lapu fighting spirit in me.

"It's definitely about resilience and holding it down for your people."

On April 27, 1521, Lapu-Lapu led native warriors against Magellan's forces at the Battle of Mactan in the Visayan islands of the Philippines. Using their knowledge of the terrain, the defenders overcame the Portuguese explorer's armed expedition and killed Magellan, disrupting Portugal's efforts to establish control over the islands.

Lapu-Lapu's victory remains a defining moment in Philippine history. He is celebrated as a symbol of Filipino resistance, courage and independence.

Parsons will carry that same resolve into his next challenge. The 35-year-old is set to face José Souza in a welterweight bout at UFC Fight Night: Cortes-Acosta vs. Walker.

"It's just a great story about overcoming the odds," Parsons said.

"They won that battle against Magellan, and in [Lapu-Lapu's] lifetime, the Philippines wasn't conquered. It wasn't until years after he was gone that they were conquered.

"I definitely want to say that my fighting spirit comes from that side of the family."

Parsons will have his own odds to overcome against Souza, as the Brazilian stands 6-foot-3 and holds a 10-inch reach advantage over the 5-foot-9 Parsons.

Souza, 24, carries a 9-1 professional record and is 1-0 in the UFC. On the other hand, Parsons owns a 9-3 record, including a 1-0 mark in the UFC.

The Filipino-American is returning from a layoff of 40 months after persistent hip flexor and groin injuries disrupted his training and kept him away from competition.

Still, he believes he has the tools to deal with the physical disadvantage and make a statement in his return.

"I'm no stranger to fighting a taller, longer opponent," he said.

"I think I have all the tools and weapons to defeat this guy [Souza].

"It just means that everyone's going to be able to see the best Jonny Parsons so far. But not the best ever, because I'm still getting better."

The extended break did not mean stepping away from the sport. Parsons, who is also now a mixed martial arts coach, kept training, shifting his focus to building strength, improving his conditioning, and addressing the physical issues that had held him back.

"This whole time that I've been off, I've been training," he told ESPN.

"I've been focusing on my strength and conditioning to help mend injuries and certain problem areas that were giving me issues during training.

"So I would say right now, I'm the healthiest and strongest I've ever been."

The experience also forced Parsons to rethink how he prepares for fights.

Rather than pushing through every session, he learned to treat recovery as seriously as training to develop a more disciplined approach to keeping his body healthy.

"I put a very heavy emphasis on my strength and conditioning training here in Vegas at the Performance Institute," he said.

"I also put much more effort into my recovery. Sometimes recovery, well, actually all the time, recovery is not just laying in bed and resting.

"Recovery is stretching. Recovery is a cold plunge, a sauna and walking. So I've really developed a much smarter training regimen that has allowed me to train at a very high level while avoiding all types of injuries."

Parsons is ready to show what that patience and discipline have produced.

"I'm very calm when I go into fights, and I'm very peaceful. I know I fight the best when I'm at peace. And it's very easy for me now to find that peace."

stories.headline: Relative obscurity to pick 1 buzz: WA's Heath Mellody is the ultimate bolter
stories.summary: Heath Mellody was a relatively unknown prospect earlier in the year. But then the National Championships came around, and the Larke Medallist suddenly has open pool pick 1 buzz, writes Jasper Chellappah.
stories.body:
Heath Mellody was sporting a new look at the AFL Draft combine. Usually standing out with the long, curly locks flying through the midfield, the Hale School graduate was hard to recognise with a buzzed dome.

He and schoolmates in Perth shaved their hair in the name of brain cancer research to venerate a Hale student.

Ryan Murphy passed away in early 2023 from glioblastoma, an incurable brain tumour. Mellody and his friends have been paying tribute ever since, with all proceeds being donated to the Harry Perkins Institute of Medical Research.

It's become a tradition at a school that has meant so much to Mellody. He opted to play his state-based footy with Hale in the PSA over the Claremont Colts.

From representing Western Australia at the national championships to running out on Optus Stadium for the WAFL Grand Final, his stocks have just kept on rising.

"School, academy, state and WAFL, it's just been so good," Mellody told ESPN.

"I love playing PSA footy with all my schoolmates. I sort of realised it'd probably be my last time playing with them.

"I didn't want to take it for granted, just tried playing like I usually would, preparing the same for any game. I loved every game and just had so much fun playing with my mates."

With no vision of the competition and no data being captured by Champion Data it kept Mellody hidden through the first portion of the season. That all changed at the National Champs.

"I was playing predominantly halfback and in the trial games I was having more of a split, and I was always playing a bit better in the midfield.

"I was always planning on playing midfield for parts of the first two games but that just didn't eventuate. But just before halftime of the Marvel game (against Vic Country) I got moved into the middle.

"I definitely prefer playing inside and it was just super fun going in there. We sort of mixed it up a bit in there and it gave us a bit more intent, bit more run and carry which in the end really helped.

WA was trailing Vic Country 38-10 before his move on-ball. They then piled on nine goals to three in the second half to storm over the top in front of every recruiter in the country.

Mellody was the firestarter. He won hard balls through the middle and used his trademark dash to put speed on the ball in transition. His hands were lightning under pressure and he had some special moments forward of centre that will be ingrained in those recruiters' minds.

The then-17-year-old finished with 33 disposals in the biggest 'pick me' game of the year.

He ended his epic champs with the Larke Medal around his neck as the best performed player at the carnival, joining the likes of Will Ashcroft, Sam Walsh and Christian Petracca by winning the award.

In truth, Mellody has been a prospect in demand since blitzing the colts grand final last season as a bottom-ager when he collected 25 touches and kicked a beautiful goal breaking the paint of 50 in a Claremont triumph.

"I loved playing Claremont colts last year. Getting connection with Charlie Banfield and Cody Curtin, playing AFL now, and going up against Toby Whan and Fred Rodriguez on Optus.

"That was so much fun and playing well in that finals series gave me a lot of confidence to go out and perform well this year."

That ended up being his final game of colts footy for Claremont because he was immediately called up to the senior team for a finals run this year. The Tigers surged from the middle of the ladder to make an unlikely grand final against a Peel side loaded with Fremantle talent.

Their best player in that grand final run was a teenager that missed his debut phone call because he was in second period at school.

"Ash [Prescott], the coach, gave me a ring while I was at school so I didn't actually pick it up. He called during the first couple periods... The head of sport at Hale told me to go get my phone and give him a call back!

"I went and did that and he was like 'Yeah, you're playing this week'."

Mellody's run at league level included a best on ground performance against a West Coast reserves midfield boasting the likes of Elijah Hewett, Fin Macrae and Harry Schoenberg. He took them to task with 34 disposals and a goal as Claremont rolled into finals.

"The biggest challenge was just working around the physicality of it. Obviously I'm a little bit smaller so it's going to be hard for me to body up so just working around that, getting off body, getting on the move a bit.

"The transition to the midfield made it a lot more comfortable for me at the level."

Mellody is now on the precipice of the top five, and has genuine pick 1 buzz. He's the most in-demand WA prospect since Luke Jackson, and West Coast is right in the mix at pick 3.

Mellody's beautiful kicking action and insatiable appetite to run and deliver is ideal for the modern game. He takes the ball from inside to out with leg drive that's reminiscent of Bailey Smith, though prides himself on his ball use going inside 50 and can pull off miraculous kicks when given space.

It may well be the Eagles who call Mellody's name, but the Bombers or Tigers will have first call on the unflappable teenager.

"I don't really have a preference to be honest. I'd just love to go anywhere, whether that be staying home or going interstate. I feel like it would be super cool and a great experience going anywhere... I've got a lot of support around Australia so I'll be able to manage if I were to move."

stories.headline: How the Atlanta Dream turned their franchise around in just five years
stories.summary: Five years ago, the Dream were the second-worst team in the WNBA -- making their Finals run all the more remarkable.
stories.body:
SAN FRANCISCO -- Just five years ago, the idea of the Atlanta Dream competing for the WNBA championship trophy would have seemed as unlikely as a rebound landing untouched next to Angel Reese.

So finishing within one victory of a title, as the Dream did in the WNBA Finals last week, says a lot about just how far the franchise has come since 2021. Even without the 2026 championship, what the Dream did in revitalizing their franchise is a story that shouldn't be lost in Golden State's celebration. Five years ago, the Dream were a mess. Now, they're contenders. That's something other WNBA franchises can look to.

"It's remarkable, really," Atlanta coach Karl Smesko said.

Consider how far the franchise was from this in 2021.

That was the year the Dream moved to Gateway Center Arena -- the smallest venue in the WNBA at 3,500 seats -- because too much of their longtime larger home (State Farm Arena, capacity 17,608) was vacant during games. The Dream had three different coaches that year, one resigning just before the season began to take a college job. Chennedy Carter, their lottery-pick selection from 2020, was suspended in July and never returned. They finished in second-to-last place in the WNBA at 8-24.

The team's most notable moment came not on court, but in a viral video of two Dream players throwing punches by a food truck outside an Atlanta nightclub.

Those were the low points. But behind the scenes, two big moves in 2021 helped spark a turnaround: an ownership change, led by real estate investor Larry Gottesdiener, and a new general manager, Dan Padover.

Reese was then a college sophomore with huge goals for her future. But it wasn't until this April that she knew those plans would intersect with the Dream.

"When I play with joy and I'm surrounded by people that just genuinely make me happy, I think I'm at my best," Reese said. "The organization has poured into me. To be in my third year [in the WNBA], this is obviously the best situation I've ever been in."

And even as Reese and teammates Jordin Canada and Allisha Gray sat somberly in the Dream's postgame news conference after Game 7, the joyful sounds of Ballhalla's celebration audible, they looked dissatisfied but not devastated.

"They changed my life," Reese said of the Atlanta players and staff. "And I'm just so grateful for them."

A 2008 EXPANSION TEAM, the Dream's first title hopes were led by another Angel -- 2009 No. 1 pick Angel McCoughtry. She led the Dream to the Finals in 2010, 2011 and 2013, but they were swept each time.

The Dream then missed the playoffs six of the next nine years. They won a then-franchise record 23 games in 2018, but lost McCoughtry to a knee injury Aug. 7 and lost 3-2 in the semifinals.

Without McCoughtry in 2019, the Dream averaged just 4,270 fans for home games, necessitating the move from State Farm Arena. That relocation was delayed a year because of the COVID-19 pandemic, when the 2020 season was in a "bubble" in Bradenton, Florida. By then, McCoughtry had left in free agency for Las Vegas.

The Dream's leadership became a focus for all WNBA players in the bubble when co-owner Kelly Loeffler sent a letter to commissioner Cathy Engelbert opposing the league's decision to display "Black Lives Matter" logos on the courts in Bradenton. Loeffler wrote "we need less -- not more -- politics in sports."

Loeffler was involved in a political race at the time, seeking to hold her U.S. Senate seat. The divide mushroomed into WNBA players campaigning for her opponent, Raphael Warnock.

"Being on the outside of the Dream looking in then, during that time everybody was rallying around them," said guard Jordin Canada, then with the Seattle Storm, of the bubble activism against Loeffler's continued ownership. "We wanted what was best for them and the W as a whole, and to see that transition into a more positive direction."

The situation was untenable, and the franchise was sold in February 2021 to Gottesdiener's group, which included former WNBA player Renee Montgomery.

"I believed the WNBA was an extraordinary opportunity, not just to grow the game of basketball," Gottesdiener said, "but to demonstrate what's possible when you invest in women."

Padover, who joined the Dream in October 2021, had worked for the Las Vegas Aces for three years, helping build the team that would become a three-time champion. He went from a franchise a step from the top to one with nowhere to go but up.

Padover started his WNBA career as a video coordinator with the New York Liberty in 2012, and he has credited former coach and GM Bill Laimbeer for helping him develop into a team executive. He cites this key from Laimbeer.

"If you can get your organization organized and you can take care of the players, you can start to establish yourself as a place that is respected," Padover said. "Under previous ownership, I think we were disorganized, and we didn't really have an identity.

"When I got here the goal was, 'Let's turn Atlanta back into a franchise that's respected throughout the WNBA community, one piece at a time, and that will allow us to be able to build something.' We started with things like player housing, staffing, and medical and player development."

THE OTHER PIECE was putting the right players and coaches in the building. Padover, who has been named the league's executive of the year three times, put his trade wizardry to use. He dealt the Nos. 3 and 14 picks in the 2022 draft and a 2023 pick swap to Washington for the No. 1 pick in 2022 to select Rhyne Howard.

"It was a huge boost of confidence," Howard said. "Obviously, when you get drafted, that means the team wants you. But to do it in the way that they did -- trading up to get me like that -- put no doubt in my mind that I was a piece that they were looking for to start this new journey, to start this new outcome that we're having."

The 6-foot-2 guard was Rookie of the Year and has since been a four-time All-Star. She averaged 17.7 points in the regular season this year and 16.3 in the playoffs. Howard won't recall Game 7 fondly -- she was limited to six points on 3-of-14 shooting -- but she took noticeable steps forward as a player in 2026, especially on defense.

Padover also got the steal of the second round in 2022 with forward Naz Hillmon, who became a full-time starter this season and has played more WNBA games than anyone from that draft class.

Subsequent huge deals came for guards Gray (2023) and Canada (2024).

"One of the things that I definitely took from Bill was not to be skittish to give up things in trades," Padover said. "If you're doing it to get a great player, it's always worth it, and don't be afraid to do that."

One of Padover's biggest moves in 2025 was bringing in Smesko, who had spent most of his career as a college coach, including 17 years at Florida Gulf Coast.

"Obviously, there was a changing landscape in college basketball, and I was at the point where a new challenge was needed," Smesko said of his decision to move to the WNBA. "It was Atlanta, and I love the city. And I thought there was the makings of a core that could compete for a championship."

Atlanta went 30-14 last season but lost in the first round of the playoffs. Padover used a trade to acquire the last key component. On April 6, the Dream obtained Reese from the Chicago Sky for future draft picks. Reese had become disillusioned with the Sky's direction and voiced her concerns near the end of the 2025 season. She believed in the Dream's vision, just as the players obtained before her did.

"I feel like the organization has gotten to a point where players want to come play for Atlanta," Gray said. "To be able to get Angel just speaks volumes of how the organization is run and how it really cares for players. The city of Atlanta is great. Great culture. The games just feel like one big family cookout, and everybody's welcome."

Reese proved to be the final and most essential ingredient. Other than a five-game skid June 24-July 4, the Dream -- who also added veteran DeWanna Bonner late in the season -- stayed consistent, finishing 30-14 again. Reese had the best offensive year of her career, averaging 16.4 points, plus 12.1 rebounds.

"She's made me look good all season long," Howard said. "And I'm sure she's going to continue to do that for the rest of her time here. Shoutout to her for coming in and being bought in. She's handled every challenge that we've thrown at her with grace."

This year's Finals games in Atlanta didn't come without hurdles -- facility conflicts with State Farm Arena meant one Finals game had to be moved up a day and another had to be played at 12:30 p.m. ET on a Thursday. But even that early game was joyful and loud, a full house of fans skipping work and school to cheer on the Dream in a must-win Game 6.

Next year, the Dream moves back to State Farm Arena full time, playing all 25 regular-season home games there.

And as disappointed as the Dream were after losing Game 7, they also immediately expressed excitement about the 2027 season.

"Just because we didn't win today doesn't mean that we won't be champions in the future," Reese said.

Those words weren't just platitudes after a disappointing ending. Next year, with every starter already signed to return, the Dream could at last win that elusive title.

"I like our chemistry and just the sisterhood that we have as a team," said Gray, who played every Finals game despite sustaining an injury on her shooting hand in the semifinals. "We actually love each other and enjoy being around each other."

stories.headline: Kiwis make crunch Ponga call for Tonga RLWC semifinal
stories.summary: Kalyn Ponga is set to complete a miraculous recovery from a broken forearm to feature in New Zealand's World Cup semi-final with Tonga.
stories.body:
Kalyn Ponga is set to make a remarkable return for New Zealand's semifinal with Tonga, 23 days after the Newcastle captain suffered a broken arm.

There were fears Ponga's tournament was over after one game when the fullback, making his Test debut in the World Cup opener against Australia on October 15, was substituted off with a forearm fracture.

Ponga hasn't played since but has remained in Kiwis camp.

And after undergoing a strenuous recovery process, the Newcastle fullback will be named on Stacey Jones' teamlist for Saturday's semifinal at McDonald Jones Stadium.

Jones confirmed Knights hooker Phoenix Crossland, who hasn't played since being suspended for his tackle on Nathan Cleary in the NRL preliminary final, will also come into his 19-man squad.

"We'll make that decision when the time comes but he'll be in our 19-man squad," Jones said.

"(Crossland) has had a really good week, he'll be part of our six-man bench and he's been part of our squad for three years now.

"It's a big boost and being then from here, from Newcastle, so it's pretty special to come back here and play for the Kiwis at their home ground.

"The main thing for him (Ponga) was making sure he ticks every box and is confident to play."

Ponga started at fullback against the Kangaroos in the tournament opener and will replace Keano Kini if Jones chooses to deploy the Newcastle No.1 from kick-off.

Jones would not be drawn on whether Ponga, who is expected to wear a protective arm guard against Tonga, would start against Tonga.

"I've never had that type of injury or anything in my career before, but I think a few of the boys Xavier Willison and Jahrome Hughes have," said captain James Fisher-Harris.

The return of Crossland and Ponga means two players originally listed in Jones's 19-man squad will miss out, with the Kiwis coach set to make a decision on Friday evening.

The Kiwis reached the semi-finals four years ago and the narrow loss to Australia in Leeds still burns Fisher-Harris, who is anticipating a strong turnout from Tongan supporters.

"We're looking forward to the battle and the crowd is always amazing," said the Warriors prop.

"We've spoken a little bit about our history and things and it comes down to moments.

stories.headline: Fantasy basketball's biggest surprise: What to make of Ty Jerome's hot start
stories.summary: Andre Snellings examines whether Ty Jerome is likely to keep up his tremendous start to the season.
stories.body:
Will the real Ty Jerome please stand up?

True story. In the months leading up to every NBA season, I project the stats for every rotation player in the league. As a quick behind the scenes, there are two broad steps included in this process for veteran players: I try to determine each player's production-per-minute based on previous seasons, then I anticipate what their playing time will look like in the upcoming season. There are some other steps as well, but at the end of the process I have a projected stat line, number of minutes and number of games for each rotation player. Once I have those, I can run the stats through the fantasy points scoring algorithm and sort by "most total points" to get an initial set of player rankings.

This season, when I finished the process and sent the rankings to my editor, I got a one-liner message about an hour later: "Ty Jerome is very high. That's the first thing I see. Do we want him that high?"

It turned out that, based on my initial projections, Jerome was coming out as a top-25 player. He's never been ranked anywhere near that high in his career, as an instant offense off the bench guy for the most part and never a full-time starter. When I dug into how he got that high, it was because his per-minute stats in recent seasons were incredible and it appeared that he was going to play starter minutes this season.

Last season, in an injury-shortened campaign, Jerome averaged 19.7 PPG and 5.7 APG in under 23 MPG. If you scale that production rate up to 30-plus minutes, it was easy to see how Jerome was projecting so high. But, in this type of situation, we have to consider other elements. How would Jerome do when, instead of coming off the bench as instant offense, he was instead the focal point of opposing defenses? And what about his durability -- he missed most of last season injured, and has only been a reserve in previous seasons -- so could I really project him to starter minutes for 70-plus games?

After some deliberation, we scaled back Jerome's estimated minutes and games played, and he moved down our preseason rankings into the 60s. Still a career-best projected ranking for him, but no longer a player projected for the top three rounds in fantasy drafts.

Then, the season began. And through the first week, Jerome led the entire NBA in scoring with averages of 34.7 PPG, 6.0 APG and 3.0 3PG. At the time of our first fantasy rankings update of the season, I told my editor I was undoing all of the limits I had included in Jerome's preseason projections. When I did so, using feedback from the current season, Jerome came out as a top-15 player in the fantasy rankings that week.

I felt good about it until later that night, when Jerome started his second week. In that second week, Jerome's numbers plummeted back to earth. In three games, he had one DNP (back), and in his two games averaged 12.5 PPG, 5.5 APG and 1.0 3PG in 27.0 MPG. And all of the questions I had about Jerome's durability and his ability to deal with star-level defensive attention came back. With more feedback from the current season, Jerome's rankings slid a bit, into the upper 30s in both points and category leagues.

Felt like the right thing to do ... until that night. The very night the rankings update went through with more conservative estimates, Jerome exploded for his second 40-point game of the season with five each of assists, rebounds and 3-pointers.

So, as we sit here a few weeks into the season, the question remains: who is the real Ty Jerome this season? Is he a player whose start is fluky, and you should consider trading him now while his value is high? Or is he a player producing exactly as expected, and if anything he should be either a hold or even a trade-for player while his reputation still doesn't fit his production level?

My answer is yes. All of the above. Read your league's situation, gauge his trade value, and make your decision accordingly. Let me explain.

When watching the Memphis Grizzlies play, Jerome has the ultimate green light in that offense. He is the lead guard while he's on the court, which means he has the ball in his hands often and he is creating his own shot off the dribble. And some of those shots can only be called "heat checks", shots that when I was playing would have gotten me taken from the game immediately if I ever attempted them.

But the Grizzlies are fine with Jerome taking those shots, and that's the next aspect of Jerome's value: he is a very streaky shooter who, when he's hot, can shoot as much as he wants. This is how Jerome is able to put these 30- and 40-point games on the board. It's also how, when he's not hot, he can have 10- and 15-point relative clunkers, because when he's off, he's off.

But averages are all about large numbers of repetitions, and in an 82-game season I expect Jerome to settle into an average that is a step down from his peaks but well above his valleys. And ultimately, the exercise of looking at Jerome's per-minute value and then projecting that to more than 30 MPG was useful in identifying his likely value this season.

Currently, Jerome ranks 25th in the ESPN Fantasy Player Rater. In standard points leagues, Jerome ranks 16th in fantasy points per game and 30th in total fantasy points. For the entirety of the season, trying to account for production ups-and-downs as well as potential injury absences, a reasonable range of fantasy values for Jerome is somewhere in the 15th to 40th range.

So, when determining Jerome's trade value, I suggest making your decisions based upon those extremes. If Jerome is on your team, and you can trade him for 15th overall value, then you strongly consider making the move. But if you can only get 40th player value for him, then he is worth holding onto.

Likewise, if you don't have Jerome on your squad and the team that has him is asking top-15 value for him, you probably hold off. But if you can trade for him for No. 40-player value, then he could be a good investment with upside.

Through the first few weeks of the season, I've seen enough to say that Jerome as an impact fantasy player is real. The projections based on his history of per-minute production were legit, and as long as he is healthy he should remain a high-impact producer this season.

Betting side note: Per DraftKings, Jerome currently has the shortest odds in the league for Most Improved Player (+250). I typically want longer odds for season-long bets, but in this case I see solid value here. The biggest question is if Jerome plays the 65-game minimum, because he has surpassed that threshold only once in his seven previous NBA seasons. But if Jerome meets the games played threshold, it is unlikely that any other player will see a bigger jump from his previous career value than Jerome will. His career averages prior to this season were 8.9 PPG and 3.0 APG, and even from last season to this we're currently looking at a big jump from 19.7 PG to 27.4 PPG. If Jerome can meet the 65-game threshold, he would seem to be in the pole position to win MIP.

stories.headline: Gianluigi Donnarumma knows he's 'made mistakes' for Man City - Enzo Maresca
stories.summary: Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca has reiterated his support for Gianluigi Donnarumma but said the Italian goalkeeper knows he's made mistakes.
stories.body:
Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca has reiterated his support for Gianluigi Donnarumma but said the Italian goalkeeper knows he's made mistakes.

Donnarumma was at fault for RB Leipzig's second goal in City's 3-2 win over the German side on Wednesday when he let Ridle Baku's tame effort sneak in at his near post.

He was almost caught out again when a second-half free-kick looped over his head and hit the crossbar.

And while Maresca gave no indication he is ready to replace the 27-year-old in goal, he acknowledged Donnarumma has made some avoidable errors.

"Overall he's good," Maresca told a news conference on Friday.

"He's quite relaxed in terms of he recognises that he has made some mistakes, but at the same time he has also made some good saves. It's just a matter of balance. Try to avoid mistakes and continue to do the right things."

Donnarumma's patchy form this season has led to questions about his place in the City team.

But Maresca has repeatedly backed the former AC Milan and Paris Saint-Germain keeper and he's expected to keep the gloves for the visit to Nottingham Forest on Saturday.

"There are players who, when they make mistakes, you need to have conversations with them and there are players who you just need eye contact," Maresca said.

"With Gigio it's easy because every time he has made something that was not correct he recognises immediately. I spoke with him, but sometimes you don't need to be so deep with some players and recognise that."

stories.headline: Houston Dynamo's Lyle Foster earns Bafana Bafana recall for Kenya AFCON qualifying double-header
stories.summary: Houston Dynamo striker Lyle Foster, on loan from Burnley, earned a recall to the Bafana Bafana squad ahead of November's 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) qualifying double-header against tournament co-hosts Kenya.
stories.body:
Houston Dynamo striker Lyle Foster, on loan from Burnley, earned a recall to the Bafana Bafana squad ahead of November's 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) qualifying double-header against tournament co-hosts Kenya.

South Africa will host Kenya at Orlando Amstel Arena on Nov. 13 before travelling for a reverse fixture against Benni McCarthy's Harambee Stars four days later.

McCarthy is Bafana's all-time record scorer with 31 goals. While he was entering the twilight of his career at Orlando Pirates (ironically the club which plays its home games in the venue the teams will square off at on Nov. 13), a young Foster was scouted by Augusto Palacios - the same coach who McCarthy's goals fired to a domestic treble in 2011-12.

Foster has been tipped as a potential heir to McCarthy atop the Bafana all-time scoring charts. However, he has struggled with inconsistent form and mental health issues and was reportedly not at full fitness for Pitso Mosimane's first three games in charge - wins over Guinea, Eritrea and Egypt.

Foster was cut from Mosimane's first preliminary squad, but this time, he has made the 27-man final list alongside his "cousin-uncle" Luther Singh.

Foster's grandmother and Singh's mother are sisters. Singh is the first cousin of Foster's father.

AEL Limassol winger Singh, 29, had been brought back into the Bafana fold by Mosimane for his first three games after falling out of favour under Hugo Broos. Foster, 26, was Broos' usual first choice upfront when available.

Elsewhere, Mosimane has opted to include goalkeeper-captain Ronwen Williams and midfielder Teboho Mokoena despite recent recurring injury struggles with Mamelodi Sundowns. However, their club teammate, Khuliso Mudau, has not recovered in time to be included at right-back.

Thabang Matuludi and the versatile Thapelo Morena - also at Sundowns - are the two right-backs in the squad, with Orlando Pirates' Kamogelo Sebelebele also missing out due to injury.

Mbekezeli Mbokazi unsurprisingly returns at centre-back after an early recovery from his own injury struggles, with Ime Okon (Hannover 96), Olwethu Makhanya (Rangers) and Lebone Seema (Orlando Pirates) the other centre-backs in the squad. This time, there is no room for Nkosinathi Sibisi (Orlando Pirates).

Mbokazi is in familiar company, with the Fire's Puso Dithejane also making the squad as expected after scoring the winner against Egypt and continuing to excel in his role as a winger/attacking midfielder for the Men in Red.
